cards.title: What you owe, and what you don't
cards.body: Today's deck keeps returning to one question: what do you really owe the people close to you, and what do you only assume you owe? The piece not to miss is Jane English on grown children and parents — she argues you owe them nothing, because love given freely was never a loan. Beauvoir asks the same of couples, and one psychology piece turns it on your own mind: when did being human become something you are supposed to treat?

cards.title: Children owe their parents friendship, not a debt
cards.body: Most of us assume a child owes their parents for years of care — a bill that comes due later. Jane English argued that debts come only from what you asked for, and nobody asks to be born. What all that sacrifice builds, she said, is not a debt but a friendship — and a friendship can end.

sections.text:
"You wouldn't be alive without me," a father says, happily, and not for the first time. "I didn't ask to be born," his grown son says back.

Most moral traditions side with the father. The Bible tells you to honour your father and mother. Confucian thought in ancient China is built around xiao — filial piety, the duty to respect and serve your parents. It is not a nice extra. It is one of the deepest duties a person has, and the base of a good life.

The case for it is warm, not bullying. Your parents fed you before you could feed yourself. They gave up sleep, money, plans. Learning to put them first is practice for being good everywhere else: you hold your own wants in check so you can live well with everyone. Two Chinese proverbs carry the feeling — one generation plants trees so a later generation can rest in the shade; when you drink the water, remember who dug the well. The order is practical, not cruel. At the start they know how to live and you do not, so you follow. Later they weaken, and you carry them. Serve your father, Confucius says, as you would want your son to serve you. You did not ask to be born? Nobody did. You are simply the newest carrier of a life handed down.

In a 1979 paper, the philosopher Jane English said this picture is built wrong. She called the target the debt theory: care given makes a bill to be paid.

Debts come from what you asked for, or agreed to. A child asked for nothing. The parents are the only side that chose — they decided to have a child and raise one. Choosing something, then taking responsibility for it, does not put the other person in your debt. Help you never asked for does not create a debt either. If a friend buys you dinner unasked, you do not now owe them a dinner. Nor do you owe your parents for the nappies they changed.

So what do those years of sacrifice build? Love, English said. Friendship. And friendship carries real duties — just not the pay-it-back kind. You listen to your parents growing up, and you help them when they need it, for the reason you would help any friend: that is what people on good terms do. Nobody keeps a ledger, a running account of who owes what.

She set two tests for what a child should do: what each side needs and can actually give, and how much real friendship is still alive between them. The duty lasts as long as the friendship lasts. If a parent disowns their child, or shows no interest in them, the child owes that parent nothing — no help, no respect, not even by default.

That is the clean version of her argument, and also the uncomfortable one. The debt was never there to be cancelled.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text:
The friendship model may miss what makes this bond unlike any other. Without these two people, you would not exist at all. And if duty depends on how the relationship is going right now, it becomes easy to leave at the worst moment: a parent hits a hard stretch, the warmth drains out, and the duties drain with it. Do the earlier years count for nothing?

Some philosophers answer that we owe no debt, but we do owe gratitude — and gratitude holds even when the relationship hurts. Our parents did not choose us in particular either; any decision to have a child is a leap of faith. If they did the best they could with what they had, we should at least try to do the same.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A debt can be cleared. A friendship has to be kept up.

recall.q: Parents give up years, money and sleep for a child. Why does English say this creates no debt — and what does she say it creates instead?
recall.a: Because debts come from what you asked for or agreed to, and no child asks to be born — the parents are the only side that chose. The sacrifice builds love and friendship, so the duties are a friend's duties, and they last only as long as the friendship does.

cards.title: Trump's own Fed pick raised rates anyway
cards.body: The US Federal Reserve — America's central bank — raised its main interest rate by 0.25 percentage points. That rate shapes borrowing costs across the whole economy. The chair who led the vote, Kevin Warsh, is Donald Trump's own pick, chosen to push those costs down. He did the opposite, and every other board member voted with him.

sections.text: August inflation came in hotter than expected. August jobs came in stronger. Warsh pointed back to his speech at Jackson Hole, the yearly meeting where central bankers explain their thinking: "trends matter." The summer inflation trend, he judged then, was failing the test. Nothing since had changed his mind. Markets took the rise in stride.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 0.25 percentage points — the size of the rise.
94% — the odds of a rise markets had already priced in, after the August inflation and jobs reports.
16 of 18 — Fed members who expect at least one more rise before the year ends.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: A central bank is called independent when it sets rates on the economy's numbers, not the president's wishes. Warsh faced a clean version of that test: unsettle investors, or break with the man who hired him to make money cheaper. He chose the data, and took the whole board with him. He would not say whether he and Trump had spoken.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Warsh refused to promise the Fed's next move. Most of his board already has. The open question is Trump. His top economic adviser, Kevin Hassett, said the White House would respect the process. Trump's allies in the Senate are louder. Sen. Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, called a rise this close to the midterm elections "not great" and said it will do nothing to lower gas prices.

recall.q: Trump picked Kevin Warsh to make borrowing cheaper. Why did Warsh raise the rate instead?
recall.a: The data. August inflation ran hotter than expected and jobs came in stronger. He had warned at Jackson Hole that the summer inflation trend was failing the test, and nothing since changed his mind. Every other board member voted with him.

cards.title: Day 1 · Every philosophy is a confession
cards.body: The book opens with a joke about courting Truth and ends up dismantling Plato, Kant, Spinoza and the Stoics — signed from Sils Maria, June 1885. Today gives you the tool the whole book runs on: stop asking whether a thought is true, and ask what kind of life needed it to be true.

sections.text:
Suppose Truth is a woman. Then all those solemn philosophers who came courting her with heavy seriousness were clumsy suitors, and she never once let herself be won. That is the opening line, and the joke has teeth. Every grand system of philosophy, he says, was actually built on something small: an old superstition, "a play upon words, a deception on the part of grammar," or a bold guess stretched out of "very personal, very human--all-too-human facts." Plato's invention of Pure Spirit and the Good in Itself was the worst of these errors, and Christianity, he adds in passing, "IS PLATONISM FOR THE 'PEOPLE'." But he is neither simply grateful nor simply angry. Two thousand years of fighting that error stretched Europe like a bow. He wants the arrow.

Then he turns on the one thing nobody thinks to question: the wish for truth itself. Philosophers have always praised their own truthfulness. Nobody asked what it is, or what it costs. The old riddle flips — we came to question the Sphinx and the Sphinx is questioning us. "Granted that we want the truth: WHY NOT RATHER untruth? And uncertainty? Even ignorance?" He notes, quietly, that there is risk in asking.

Behind every metaphysician (someone who claims to know what is finally, really real) sits one shared faith: "THE BELIEF IN ANTITHESES OF VALUES." True against false, generous against selfish — as if the good things must come from a separate, pure source, never from this messy world. Maybe they are not opposites at all. Maybe the respected things are "insidiously related, knotted, and crocheted" to the ugly ones, even "essentially identical" with them. Our confident rankings may be "frog perspectives" — the view from low down, from one corner.

Why do we hold them so hard? Because most conscious thinking is instinct wearing a suit. Behind logic sit "physiological demands, for the maintenance of a definite mode of life." So he changes the test. Not: is this opinion true? But: does it keep this kind of creature alive? "The falseness of an opinion is not for us any objection to it." Numbers, fixed things, an imagined world of the absolute — counterfeits we cannot live without. Admit untruth as a condition of life, and by that act alone your thinking has placed itself beyond good and evil. The title is not a slogan. It is a description of a move.

Here is the part worth stealing. Philosophers pose as if their conclusions arrived through "cold, pure, divinely indifferent dialectic." In fact the conclusion came first — "their heart's desire abstracted and refined" — and the arguments were "sought out after the event." "They are all advocates who do not wish to be regarded as such." Kant, stiff and decent, walking us into his moral law. Spinoza clothing his thought in mathematics like armour, "mail and mask," to terrify anyone who looks too closely — which tells you mostly about his "personal timidity and vulnerability."

And he is enjoying this. Epicurus mocked Plato's school as Dionysiokolakes: tyrant's flatterers, and in street slang, actors — "They are all ACTORS, there is nothing genuine about them" — while Epicurus himself sat in a little garden writing three hundred books, perhaps out of envy. The Stoics get it worse. Live "according to Nature"? "what fraud of words!" Nature is wasteful and "without pity or justice." Living is the opposite of that: "valuing, preferring, being unjust, being limited." They stared at Nature until they saw only Stoicism in it. Any philosophy that believes in itself does this. "It always creates the world in its own image" — the most spiritual Will to Power.

The same knife cuts Kant's famous answer. How is knowledge-before-experience possible? By means of a faculty. That is Molière's doctor explaining that opium makes you sleep because it has sleep-making power: the question repeated, not answered. Ask instead why we need to believe such things. Then the soul: throw out the soul as an eternal indivisible pebble, but keep the question open — "mortal soul," "soul as social structure of the instincts and passions." And the line the rest of the book stands on: a living thing does not first want to survive, it wants to spend its strength. "Life itself is WILL TO POWER."

Fourteen short sections in, almost nothing is left standing — except the question he has handed you about your own certainties.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: It has gradually become clear to me what every great philosophy up till now has consisted of--namely, the confession of its originator, and a species of involuntary and unconscious auto-biography; and moreover that the moral (or immoral) purpose in every philosophy has constituted the true vital germ out of which the entire plant has always grown. Indeed, to understand how the abstrusest metaphysical assertions of a philosopher have been arrived at, it is always well (and wise) to first ask oneself: "What morality do they (or does he) aim at?"

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: When an argument feels like pure logic, look for the wish it was built to defend — starting with your own.

recall.q: Nietzsche says the falseness of an opinion is not, by itself, an objection to it. So what test does he put in its place — and what does passing it cost?
recall.a: The test becomes whether an opinion is life-furthering and life-preserving, not whether it is true. He argues our most necessary beliefs (fixed things, numbers, the absolute) are useful counterfeits — and that recognising untruth as a condition of life is what puts a philosophy "beyond good and evil."

cards.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche · Helen Zimmern tr. · public domain

cards.title: A 10-second video, rebuilt from a mouse's brain cells
cards.body: Scientists recorded single cells in a mouse's visual cortex — the part of the brain that handles sight — and used that activity to rebuild the ten-second video the mouse was watching. It even worked on a clip the system had never seen before. The picture is blurry and shows only part of the scene. But nothing was copied: the image was worked out from the pattern of firing cells.
cards.evidence: single study · mice · single-cell calcium imaging of visual cortex · 10-second clips

sections.text:
Two films play side by side. On the left, ten seconds of video a mouse watched. On the right, ten seconds nobody filmed. That second movie started as a blank screen. Then it was pushed, pixel by pixel, until it matched the activity of single cells in the mouse's brain. It is blurry and shows less of the scene. But the two films run almost in step.

Here is the strange part. The system had never seen that clip. The team at University College London kept it out of the training data. They played it to the mouse, recorded its brain, and the rebuilt film still looked like it. So this was not memory. An image was being worked out from a pattern of firing cells.

That sounds like mind reading. It is not, and the reason is in the setup. At the centre is an encoding model — a program that guesses, cell by cell, how neurons will fire while a mouse watches a movie. It also uses the animal's movements and the width of its pupils. To build that model you need the one thing mind reading can never have: recordings of this mouse's own cells, made while it watched movies the team had chosen.

The model runs forward — movie in, cell activity out — so you can turn the question around. The team asked it what these cells should do if the mouse faced a blank screen. Then they compared that guess with what the cells really did. The gap between the two is the work the real movie was doing. A program then nudged the pixels of a blank film, again and again, until the predicted activity closed that gap.

The more single cells they included, the better the match. That is the tell: the picture is built from what many cells report together, not pulled off a shelf.

What the method cannot do yet is see clearly. The detail is poor, and only part of the scene comes back. It also does not travel. The model is built around one set of recorded cells, so you cannot point it at any brain.

Still, the blur may not be the failure worth watching. Sight is not a camera. The brain filters and changes what comes from the eyes, and nobody knows exactly where along the way that happens. Joel Bauer, who led the work, wants to measure it: put the world and the brain's version of it side by side, and look at the difference. He calls that difference not an error but "a feature" — a sign of how minds read into what the senses send.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: One study, in mice. The encoding model at its heart came from another team's work for a 2023 modelling competition, and the UCL group refined it on the same dataset. The rebuilt films were scored by pixel correlation — matching pixels in the real and rebuilt film one by one — which showed only small gaps in timing. The researchers themselves say the detail and how much of the scene is captured both need a lot of work. None of this was done in a human. Human attempts still rely on whole-brain scans, which are far rougher.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The picture was never the prize. The gap between it and the world is.

recall.q: The system rebuilt a video clip it had never been trained on. Why is that still not mind reading?
recall.a: Because the model is trained on recordings from that one mouse's own cells, made while it watched movies the team had chosen. It learns how those particular cells respond, then hunts for the movie whose predicted activity matches the real activity. Point it at another brain and it has nothing to work with.

cards.title: Tolkien couldn't explain enchantment, so he made one
cards.body: Tolkien spent two years failing to write a short introduction to a book he loved. Then he quit and wrote a fairy story instead. In its closing note he finally says what enchantment is: not magic, but feeling sorrow and delight for a thing at the same time. What blocks it is not a dull world. It is the belief that you already know the world.

sections.text:
In 1964 a publisher asked J.R.R. Tolkien for a few pages: an introduction to George MacDonald's The Golden Key. He loved the book and had praised it in print. He said yes. Two years later he still had not finished it.

The trouble was not the book. It was the job. Tolkien believed all his life that an introduction steals the one thing worth having — meeting a story cold, with nobody at your shoulder telling you how to feel. He had agreed to do exactly that. So he withdrew.

But two years of work had left him with a question he could not put down. He had found it necessary, he told a friend, to deal with the problem of fairy. He could not explain enchantment from outside, so he made one. Smith of Wootton Major came out in 1967, a fairy story with a note at the end. There he finally set the thing down. He spells it Faery, and means the whole enchanted world.

What he lands on has nothing to do with magic. Enchantment is two feelings held at once: ruth and delight. Ruth is an old word for pity or grief. It comes from the Old English hrēow, sorrow. It gives us the verb to rue, and today it survives mostly inside ruthless. Sorrow for a thing, joy in the same thing, together. That is not an escape from life. It is feeling life across its whole range.

Both halves come from one love — a love that does not want to own what it loves, that lets it stay other than you. What shuts that love off is not a dull world. It is two rings. The weaker is "the iron ring of the familiar". The stronger is "the adamantine ring of belief that it is known, possessed, controlled" — and so the only thing worth bothering with. Adamantine means diamond-hard.

Your ride to work sits inside both. You have done it enough times that your eyes stop reporting: the same overbridge, the same shutters, the same man setting out his cart. The iron ring is only boredom, and boredom you can live with. The adamantine ring does the damage — the settled belief that you are finished with this road, that looking again would give you nothing. That belief is a fact about you, not about the road.

This is not the same as being told to notice more. Cynicism, pessimism and optimism share one flaw: each has already decided how the world is. Enchantment is the truer realism, because it stays open to a world that keeps outgrowing the ring. Tolkien puts it beside sunlight — as necessary for a person working fully as light is for a living body. And the world inside the ring beat long odds to exist. It did not have to be here at all.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: You do not need a different road. You need to stop believing you are done with this one.

recall.q: Tolkien names two rings that shut enchantment out. Which one is the harder problem, and why does it matter on a road you already know?
recall.a: The iron ring of the familiar is the weaker one. The harder is the adamantine ring — the belief that the world is known, possessed, controlled, and so the only thing worth bothering with. A familiar road only bores you; believing you are finished with it stops you from looking at all, and that is a fact about you, not the road.

cards.title: Chimps hand tools to their young, at a cost
cards.body: Camera traps in Senegal caught 33 moments where one wild chimp ended up holding another chimp's tool. The tools moved from skilled users to less skilled ones, and in 30 percent of cases from a mother to her own child. The young ones then fished longer and ate more. The giver's own meal usually stopped right there.
cards.evidence: single study · 33 tool transfers · ~15 hours of camera-trap footage · one wild population

sections.text:
The stick is already in the ant nest when Saïsaï gets to it. She did not put it there. Her mother, Soukki, slid the thin stick down into the nest, left it standing, then brought her baby daughter over. Saïsaï pulls it out. It comes up coated in ants, and she eats them.

Almost nothing you know, you worked out yourself. Skills reach you already made, and you spend a life adding small things to them. Researchers call this cumulative culture — knowledge that piles up across generations instead of dying with each individual. How much of this happens outside our own species? Nobody knows yet. A new study of wild chimps in Senegal is one small, concrete piece of the answer.

Researchers from the University of Barcelona and the Jane Goodall Institute set camera traps at 25 spots in the Dindefelo savanna, where chimps go to fish out ants, termites and algae. (A camera trap is a camera that switches on by itself when something moves in front of it.) About 15 hours of footage came back. In it were 33 moments where one chimp watched another feed, then ended up holding that chimp's tool.

Which way the tools moved matters more than the count. They mostly went from skilled users to less skilled ones, and in 30 percent of cases from mothers to their own young. After getting a tool, the young ones spent significantly more time fishing, and took more mouthfuls of food. For the giver, the handover usually ended the meal, or cut it sharply. Passing the tool cost them their own food.

Now be exact about "handed down". The cameras did not follow a technique down a family line over years. They caught an object moving from one animal to another, 33 times. The generational part is read from the pattern — who gives, who receives — not watched as it happened.

What lifts Soukki's stick above plain sharing is that she changed her own behavior to set the moment up. Lead author Andreu Sánchez-Megías argues that teaching needs "an active role from the teacher", and that teaching evolves for information too complex to pick up by watching alone. Loading a stick, then fetching the learner, is that active role, on film.

The tools are clearly worth having. The same cameras caught a couple of thefts: a chimp grabbing at another's tool, a scuffle, the owner swinging at the thief.

So go back to the stick in the ant nest. Saïsaï could not have invented it. She did not need to.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is 15 hours of footage from one population, in one place, and 33 transfers is a small number. Camera traps only see what walks into frame — a chimp that shares out of view never shared, as far as the data goes. The write-up says the young ones fished significantly longer, but gives no figures. And whether any of these tools carry a technique no single chimp could have worked out alone is exactly what this study did not test.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Nobody starts from nothing — and that may not be a human privilege.

recall.q: The study is described as chimps handing tools down across generations. What did the cameras actually record, and what did they not?
recall.a: They recorded a tool physically passing from one chimp to another 33 times, mostly from skilled users to less skilled ones, and in 30 percent of cases from a mother to her own offspring. They did not follow any technique down a family line over years — the generational claim is read from the pattern of who gives and who receives.

cards.title: India cleared 642 UK cars in 63 days. Quota: 10,480.
cards.body: India has approved 642 cars from the United Kingdom under the new trade deal — 63 days in, or about ten cars a day. This year's quota is a reported 10,480 cars. So the deal is moving, but on a short leash. Inside the quota, the import duty falls from as high as 110% to 30%. Outside it, nothing has changed.

sections.text:
India has cleared 642 cars from the UK at a lower duty. That is 63 days after the India-UK trade pact, called CETA, took effect on 15 July 2026 — about ten cars a day.

The tool is a tariff-rate quota, or TRQ: a set number of cars get the cheap tax, and every car after that pays the full rate. Eight companies applied, seven were given quota, and one was told its paperwork fell short. Only carmakers and their approved dealers could apply, with a purchase agreement already in place and a UK certificate of origin.

The deal began mid-year, so 2026's share is scaled down to a reported 10,480 cars. Against that, 642 is about 6%. The duty cut is real and steep. It is also counted, capped, and — for electric cars — not there at all until year six.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 20,000 petrol and diesel cars in a full first year; about 10,480 for 2026 after the part-year cut
110% duty falls to 30% for petrol above 3,000cc and diesel above 2,500cc
66% falls to 50% for smaller and mid-size engines
378,000 cars over 15 years, peaking at 37,000 in year five, then tapering, with duties phased down to 10%

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: A quota is not an open market. CETA has made a fixed, named set of UK cars much cheaper to land in India. Everything past that set still pays the old tariff. The 10% headline duty is the end point of a 15-year climb-down, not today's rate. And the quota for electric, hybrid and hydrogen vehicles does not open until year six, with cheaper models protected to shield India's own EV industry.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Whether the first application window, aimed at roughly 5,000 units or more, fills by the end of the year. That is the first honest test of demand, not of the paper size of the quota.

recall.q: Why is it wrong to measure the 642 cars against the 20,000-car quota?
recall.a: 20,000 is the full-year number. CETA started mid-year, on 15 July 2026, so 2026's quota is scaled down to a reported 10,480 cars. Against what is actually available this year, 642 is about 6%.

cards.title: When did being human become something to treat?
cards.body: Distress has social causes. The new culture treats it as a private project to manage — and a diagnosis as something to build an identity from. Therapist Julie Tilsen names two forces behind the flip: ordinary parts of being alive renamed as illness, and harm done by governments and markets handed back to us as our own problem to fix. Her target is not therapy, but the culture that keeps sending therapy work it cannot do.

sections.text:
Ten years ago, no self-respecting teenager wanted a diagnosis. Now, says the therapist Julie Tilsen, people build their whole sense of self around one. Her book Personal Responsibility, Inc. asks how that flip happened.

The old deal was adjustment. Being responsible meant growing into a normal adult: fit in, hold steady, do not make a scene. The pressure came from outside — public opinion strong enough to keep everyone in place by keeping them normal.

The new deal is not fitting in. It is improving, forever. Be your "best self" — a phrase Tilsen notes we got from Oprah. The order arrives from every direction at once: social media, your doctor, your therapist. Manage yourself, regulate yourself, keep it together. The line moves as you reach it, so the work never closes. And nobody has to enforce it. You are already watching yourself.

Two things drove the switch, she argues. The first is medicalization — treating an ordinary part of being alive as a medical problem. Still grieving three months after a death? Illness. A child who hates worksheets and cannot sit at a desk for six hours? Illness.

The second is that the real conditions of a person's life get hidden. Harm done by governments, systems and moneyed interests is made private, turned into your own problem to solve. Then your response to the harm is treated as an illness, and you are sent to therapy for it. The band of normal narrows until almost nobody fits, and therapy becomes routine, like drinking water or taking a multivitamin.

But Tilsen will not let the old side look innocent. Grow up, adjust, be normal was never a universal human standard. It was one culture's idea of adulthood — modern, European, from one stretch of history. And normal always hides a question: normal compared to what, decided by whom, and who is left outside the answer?

Therapy, she says, has always been partly a tool of social control, because it grows out of a culture and rarely sees past that culture's edges. Diagnoses have always been a way to mark what is acceptable. So this is not a good past ruined by a bad present. It is one form of control traded for another, and the new one lives inside you.

Which is why diagnosis-as-identity worries her most. Two therapists who work with people's life stories, Sanni Paljakka and Tom Stone Carlson, call diagnoses "unstories": ready-made, off-the-shelf, almost brands. A diagnosis is a conversation stopper, a dead end.

Her alternative is not a better standard of normal. Responsibility is not a choice between yourself and everyone else, she says. Ask instead: responsible to whom, and for what? We can be responsible for other people because we are connected, not separate. Following the thinker Mikhail Bakhtin, she treats identity as many-sided and moving, made between people rather than fixed inside one — not what you produce, but what you contribute and what it does in the world.

What she wants back is smaller and harder than self-improvement. We are not good at sitting with discomfort, she says, our own or anyone else's. Meeting it with compassion and solidarity, instead of handing over a label, is the part that has gone missing.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The obvious reply: therapy did not cause this, and Tilsen knows it. She practises it herself, and her own argument says therapy reflects the culture it comes from — so it can hardly be blamed for that culture. A therapist who takes a person's pain seriously is often offering a kindness nobody else does. So her charge is narrower than it sounds: therapy has been handed a job it cannot do, taking in one person at a time harm that was done to everyone at once.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A diagnosis tells you what you are. A story leaves you something still to write.

recall.q: Tilsen will not call the old idea of responsibility — grow up, adjust, be normal — the good version. Why does that matter to her argument?
recall.a: Because her point is not that a good past was ruined. Both versions control people, and diagnoses have always marked what is acceptable. What changed is where the control sits — once in public opinion, now inside you — and that the social causes of distress are hidden and handed back as your private problem.

cards.title: Every question has already decided part of the answer
cards.body: A question feels like an empty box waiting to be filled. It is not. Before anyone answers, the wording has already settled what we are talking about, what kind of event it was, and what a real answer must look like. Everyone who answers agrees to all of it.

sections.text:
A building has burned. Someone stands in the wet ash with a notebook and asks the first question: How did it catch fire?

That question has already decided three things. Everyone who answers agrees to all three without noticing.

Take it apart, word by word.

It — the fire has one subject, the building. Nobody will now ask about the shop next door, or the wiring in the street.

Caught — the fire happened to the building. A question about how it was set would point at a person. Caught points at an accident.

How — the answer has to be a process. A spark, a heater left on, old wiring. If a man with a can of petrol is the true answer, this question has no room for him. He is not a how. He is a who.

Three words, three decisions, before anyone has spoken.

The move works on any question. Every question marks off two areas: what is settled and what is open. The settled part is invisible, because the question is not asking about it. The open part feels like the whole question. Answer it well or answer it badly — either way you have signed off on the settled part. A question is never a neutral tool.

Lani Watson's new book Q says we have this backwards. Our culture treats a question as a thing to get past, a step on the way to the answer. School rewards the correct answer and rarely teaches anyone how to ask. Ian James Kidd, reviewing the book, remembers being told once or twice that he asked a good question. He cannot recall a single class that taught him how. Watson sets out what questions actually do: start an inquiry, mark what we do not understand, point attention somewhere, expose assumptions. She wants readers to become "empowered questioners".

Now the boundary. The lesson is not to strip the assumptions out. You cannot. A question with nothing settled asks nothing. What? is not a better question than How did it catch fire? It is a worse one. The assumptions are what make a question usable. They are why an answer can be short.

The real skill is smaller and harder. Notice which assumptions you have granted, and check whether you meant to. Most of the time you did. The interesting cases are the ones where you did not.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: Who made the decision? — settles that a decision was made, and that one person made it. A room full of people drifting into it has no answer here.
Why didn't you reply? — settles that a message arrived, that you saw it, and that silence needs a defence.
Should we go with option A or option B? — settles that there are two options, and that one of them is going to happen.
How do I get better at this job? — settles that staying in the job is the plan.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The part of a question nobody argues with is the part doing the most work.

recall.q: How did it catch fire? has no room for a man with a can of petrol. What have its words already decided — and why can't a better answer fix that?
recall.a: Caught makes the fire something that happened to the building, not something a person did. How demands a process as the answer, not a person. Every answer given inside the question accepts both, so the fix has to be a different question.

cards.title: Senate AI safety bill nears a vote with no public text
cards.body: Senators from both parties are writing an AI safety bill. A committee could vote on it within weeks. It has not been introduced yet. Everything known about it comes from senators describing it out loud.

sections.text:
Ted Cruz chairs the Senate Commerce Committee. He said he would love to mark it up this month if the two sides agree. A markup is the meeting where a committee changes a bill and votes it out.

Amy Klobuchar is working out the text with Maria Cantwell and others. She said the bill covers "getting approvals, presenting your models to government experts, [and] alerting of imminent harm". Both Democrats call it a narrow first step; broader AI rules would wait for a later bill. Majority Leader John Thune, who is in the talks, said it is still unclear whether the bill reaches a vote at all.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Cantwell described the bill as the federal government starting to learn the risks, not setting rules for them. OpenAI's chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, said the company would back any federal AI safety effort that could pass. Anthropic gave feedback on the bill but took no position.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: The bill must be introduced and scheduled before Congress leaves for the midterm campaign; the House goes home Wednesday until November. People close to the talks name three problems still in the way: Senate politics, the White House — Trump has posted against AI rules, which Klobuchar called unhelpful — and support from the AI safety community. Any one of the three could end it.

recall.q: The bill could get a committee vote within weeks. What does it still not have?
recall.a: A text. It has not been introduced, so everything known about it comes from senators describing it out loud: getting approvals, presenting models to government experts, and alerting of imminent harm.

cards.title: After 50, the brain swaps out its oldest immune cells
cards.body: Microglia, the brain's cleaning and immune cells, form before birth. The old assumption was that the same ones stay with you for life. In the human hippocampus — the memory region — they fall away sharply between about 50 and 75, replaced by cells that look like immune cells from the blood. This is not a slide. It is a shift.
cards.evidence: single study · human hippocampus tissue · single-cell genomics · sample size not stated

sections.text:
Before you were born, your brain built its own immune cells. They are called microglia, and they are the housekeeping crew: they clear waste and keep the tissue in order. The old assumption was simple. The ones you got before birth stay with you for life.

A new study in the journal Science tested that in human tissue. Researchers read gene activity one cell at a time in the hippocampus — the brain region we use for learning and memory — in adults across a wide range of ages. What they saw was not a slow fade. It was a handover, and it runs to a rough schedule.

Before birth: microglia form. This is the start of the clock everyone assumed never ran out.

Midlife: the control settings start to move. Which genes get switched on and off begins to change broadly — decades before any symptom.

Roughly 50 to 75: the microglia formed before birth drop away sharply. In their place come cells that look, molecule by molecule, like immune cells from the blood. The brain's caretakers are being swapped for something that resembles an outsider.

The same window: those replacements carry stronger inflammation markers. That makes them a possible source of the low, constant inflammation of the ageing brain — a possibility the authors raise, not a fact they prove.

Also in that window: the cells that maintain the blood-brain barrier — the filter that keeps harmful things in the blood out of brain tissue — drop steeply. Two defences thin at once.

Across several cell types: the folded shape of DNA breaks down. DNA is not packed into the nucleus at random. It is folded into a shape that helps decide which genes are on. With age that shape gets less orderly — the filing system losing its order, not one drawer failing.

Age is the biggest known risk factor for Alzheimer's, and nobody could explain why, step by step. Bing Ren, one of the lead researchers, puts it plainly: when microglia stop doing their housekeeping, toxic material builds up and can trigger inflammation. His co-author Xiangmin Xu reads the map as a timetable for treatment — if you know when a system is rebuilt, you know when to step in.

But the window is not yours. It is drawn from many different adults at many different ages, laid side by side into a curve. That curve can say when the change tends to happen across people. It cannot say whether it has begun in you, or how fast it will move when it does.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one study, and much of it rests on resemblance. The new cells look like blood immune cells by their molecular features, which is not proof of where they came from. The stronger inflammation markers raise a possibility: the authors say these cells could add to the inflammation of the ageing brain, not that they do. And the ages come from samples taken across many adults, so the timeline is a pattern seen across people, not a path anyone was followed along.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The brain you carry at seventy is not the one you were issued. Some of the staff have been replaced.

recall.q: The study found the brain's earliest immune cells dropping away between about 50 and 75. Why does that count as a changeover rather than a decline?
recall.a: Because the cells are replaced, not just lost. The job is refilled by cells that look like immune cells from the blood, carrying stronger inflammation markers. Other systems shift in the same window: the cells that maintain the blood-brain barrier drop, and DNA folding loses its order. That is coordinated rebuilding, not one thing running down.

cards.title: Hegel in the brain lab: is dialectic just feedback?
cards.body: A philosopher wants neuroscience flipped: explain the brain with the mind, not the mind with the brain. The word holding the idea up is Hegel's dialectic. A skeptic can fairly ask if that is just an old name for a feedback loop. The reply is sharper than the objection — and may still not change a single experiment.

sections.text:
"Give it to me in one sentence," the skeptic says. "No Hegel yet."

Fine. Neuroscience has the arrow pointing the wrong way. On the Brain Inspired podcast, Paul Middlebrooks talks with Andrea Gambarotto, a philosopher at the University of Luxembourg. The argument: use minds to explain brains, not brains to explain minds.

The allies here are an odd pair. One is enactivism — the view that a mind is not a thing sitting inside a skull, but something a living body does while keeping itself alive in a world. The other is Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. What they share, Gambarotto says, is agency first: start with the whole creature doing something, then ask what the parts add.

"Then let's talk about the word you need," the skeptic says. "Dialectic. It means a thing grows by running into whatever opposes it, and changing because of the clash. My thermostat does that. The room cools, the gap is noticed, the heater fires. Engineers call it feedback and they have equations for it. What does your word add?"

"Take the version neuroscience already likes. The predictive brain: the brain is always guessing what comes next, comparing the guess with what arrives, fixing itself on the difference. That is feedback, and you are right that the machinery is old. But look at what makes a correction a correction. Someone else set the thermostat's number, and nothing is at stake for the thermostat if the room goes cold. A living thing sets its own target, and the target is itself — keep going, stay whole. The gap counts as an error only because there is somebody for whom it is one."

"That is poetry, not a difference."

"Then here is a flat one. Feedback pulls a system back to a set point that stays put. The number it aims at does not move. In the dialectical version, the clash moves the set point. The creature that hit the obstacle is not the creature that walks away from it; it now needs something slightly different. The loop does not restore. It builds."

The skeptic nods, then lands it. "Control engineers already have moving set points. Learning systems change their own targets. So you have described something we already model, and named it after a philosopher. An analogy that explains nothing new is decoration. Give me one experiment that comes out differently on your view — not one that gets described differently afterwards."

There may not be one. Agency first is a frame, not a finding. It changes which question counts as answered. It does not change the numbers coming off the machine.

What the frame does is block a habit. Say a brain area tracks reward, or represents a face. You have already helped yourself to a whole animal that wants things and looks at faces. The mental words are carrying the explanation; the brain area only borrows them. Explaining the mind by the brain quietly runs on a mind borrowed at the start. Turning the arrow around is not a result. It is a demand to pay for what you borrowed.

And the skeptic's question is still on the table. A frame that never touches a measurement is hard to tell apart from a habit of speech. So what would a neuroscience that began with the whole acting animal actually put on its screen — and would anyone still call it neuroscience?

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Every time we say a brain area represents something, a mind lent it the word.

recall.q: The skeptic says dialectic is just feedback with a philosopher's name on it. What flat difference does the expert offer — and why does the skeptic still win?
recall.a: Feedback pulls a system back to a set point that stays put; in the dialectical version the clash moves the set point, so the creature walks away needing something different. The skeptic still wins because engineers already model moving targets, and no experiment comes out differently — agency first changes which question counts as answered, not the data.

cards.title: A sound at the right moment rinses a sleeping brain
cards.body: MIT researchers played 50-millisecond bursts of sound to sleeping volunteers, each burst timed to the peak of a slow brain wave. The brain waves grew bigger — and so did the waves of fluid that wash the day's waste out of the brain. As far as the team knows, no one had a way to raise that flow on purpose before.
cards.evidence: single study · n=14 healthy adults · EEG + fMRI during sleep

sections.text:
A short sound plays in a dark scanner room. It lasts fifty milliseconds, shorter than a blink, and nobody wakes. Inside the sleeping head a wave of electricity swells. A slow tide of fluid swells with it, rinsing the brain a little harder than it would on its own.

Before you read on, guess the sound. Nothing strange — it is something you could play tonight.

Most guesses point one way. Silence, because quiet is what sleep wants. A fan's hum, a slow lullaby, waves on a beach: the sounds people already use to drift off. Every guess assumes the job is to calm the sleeper. That is not the job here.

The sound is pink noise. Like white noise, it holds every pitch the ear can hear. But the low pitches play louder and the high ones softer, so it feels gentle instead of hissy — steady rain, or a far-off waterfall. And the sound is only half the answer. The other half is when it arrives.

Deep sleep runs on slow waves: big, unhurried pulses of electrical activity. They appear only in non-REM sleep and grow strongest in its deepest stages. In 2019, Laura Lewis's lab found something else moving in step with them. Cerebrospinal fluid — the clear liquid that cushions the brain, feeds it glucose, and carries off the day's waste, things like lactic acid and worn-out proteins — washes in and out in waves locked to those slow waves.

Earlier work had shown that a sound landing right on the peak of a slow wave makes that wave bigger. Lewis reaches for a swing: push a child at the right point in the arc and the swing goes farther. The hard part, she says, is finding "just the right time" inside a sleeping brain.

They found it. In fourteen sleeping volunteers, the timed bursts made the slow waves taller, and the fluid waves rose with them. The fMRI also showed why the two travel together. Each slow wave makes blood vessels squeeze and widen, and those vessels act as a pump that drives fluid out of the brain. Push the electrical wave harder and the pump strokes harder.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: Timing was the whole engineering problem. EEG sensors read the brain waves; fMRI watches the fluid — but the magnetic fields that make an fMRI work scramble the EEG signal. The team built a way to strip that noise out in under 100 milliseconds. Even that was too slow to catch a peak as it happened, so they added an algorithm that predicts when the next peak will arrive and fires the burst just ahead of it.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Fourteen healthy volunteers, one study. It measured two things: the size of the brain waves and the size of the fluid waves. Nobody tested whether these sleepers woke feeling better, remembered more, or cleared more amyloid — the protein that builds up in Alzheimer's. Those are questions the team hopes to ask next, not answers it has. The lead author has also started a company to build a home version, something like a headband.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A sound you never hear, pushing a wave you never feel.

recall.q: Pink noise is ordinary, and the bursts were too quiet to wake anyone. So what actually made them work?
recall.a: The timing. Each 50-millisecond burst landed on the peak of a slow brain wave — like pushing a swing at the right point in its arc — so the wave grew bigger. Bigger slow waves squeeze and widen blood vessels harder, and those vessels pump more cerebrospinal fluid through the brain.

cards.title: Royce: a family needs other families nearby
cards.body: In 1886 Josiah Royce asked why families in gold-rush San Francisco kept breaking apart. His answer was not weak character. It was that each household stood alone — and a family, he wrote, grows best in a garden with its kind.

sections.text:
Ten or eleven at night, and the San Francisco merchant is still at his accounts. As soon as light shows over Mount Diablo the next morning, he begins again. He is young, he works with his brain and not his hands, and he gets no real rest.

Josiah Royce grew up in that California and wrote its history. One thing puzzled him: marriages there broke often and easily, and whole families came apart. The easy explanation was that the people were bad. Royce refused it.

The trouble, he decided, "might be said to lie in the lonesomeness of the families of a new land. The family grows best in a garden with its kind. Where family life does not involve healthy friendship with other families, it is apt to be injured by unhealthy if well-meaning friendships with wanderers."

Read it slowly. The lonesome thing in that first line is not a person. It is a family. A house can be full of people and still be the only house of its kind for streets around. That is the unit Royce is measuring.

A garden with its kind: not a wild field, not one plant in a pot. A garden is many of the same thing, in one place, over years. Community here is not a warm feeling. It is a surrounding. You stand in it, or you don't.

Then the two kinds of friendship. Healthy friendship with other families means households whose ordinary weeks overlap. Against that he sets friendships with wanderers — the single men, passing through, who were most of the city. Notice that he calls them well-meaning. He is not naming villains. His point is about balance: when the only company around is people with nothing to lose, a household slowly takes their shape.

And he is arguing, quietly, with his own city. San Francisco believed a man's vices were his own business, "a private concern between his own soul and Satan." The garden sentence denies that. What the street allows comes through your door. A family is not a sealed thing that stands or falls on its own strength.

The sentence hides something too. With its kind sounds harmless, and Royce never asks what it shuts out. Elsewhere he wants a clean, respectable neighbourhood for respectable families, safe from the wrong sort — the same logic that sorts a city and keeps people out. The line that names loneliness can also excuse a wall.

Look at the pages around this passage. Rents at figures out of the Arabian Nights. Young people working with their brains, sitting still, late into the night. Very few children. A leave-everyone-alone attitude that passes for freedom. He is describing San Francisco in the 1850s, and also, uncomfortably, a lot of expensive cities today.

A piece here recently argued that the modern trouble is less that people feel lonely and more that they are alone. Royce measures one level up. Not the person but the household — and what stands around it.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The question is not how strong your home is. It is what is growing beside it.

recall.q: In Royce's sentence, what is the lonesome thing — and why does that change his explanation?
recall.a: The family, not the person. He is not saying husbands and wives felt lonely inside the house. He is saying the household had no other households around it. That moves the cause from private character to the shape of the neighbourhood.

cards.title: Beauvoir: the best couples stay two whole people
cards.body: Beauvoir thought the devotion we praise in love — giving yourself up completely — is self-denial in a good costume. Her test for real love is strict: it should make both people larger, not melt them into one. She argued that a couple who end up thinking exactly alike lose the spark they merged to protect.

sections.text:
You wrote that the two of you finish each other's sentences now. You said it like good news.

Under that sits a fear worth taking seriously. You suspect that keeping anything for yourself — your own taste, your own view on something that matters, an evening that is yours alone — is selfish. That real love hands everything over. That the person who stays themselves loves less. Almost nobody argues with you about this. Simone de Beauvoir did.

She was writing in Paris in the 1940s and 50s. For a man, marriage was one part of a life. For a woman it was the point of one — she needed it to survive, for money and for a place in the world. So the ideal handed to her was devotion and sacrifice: disappear into the role of wife and mother, and let the rest of you go quiet. We all grow up inside stories like that, Beauvoir said, and they hide from us what we could become. They make a role feel natural instead of chosen.

Her name for living that way is bad faith, which in plain words means self-denial — you shrink what is possible for you and hand your choices over to other people's opinions. Total devotion is the sneakiest version, she thought, because it never looks like self-denial. It looks like selflessness. It looks like duty.

Everything she says about love rests on one line: "To will oneself free is also to will others free." To will something is to want it and choose it. If your own freedom matters, you cannot treat theirs as smaller. And your half is the reverse: if theirs matters, you do not get to hand yours away as a gift.

In The Second Sex she describes love as two freedoms meeting and then continuing — continuing, not closing — held by give and take, free choice and respect. Differences are not the enemy. They only have to stay differences, instead of hardening into a ladder where one of you always gets more room, more power, more possible futures.

She also thought merging takes away the very thing you merged for. A couple can be a real we with both people still inside it. But when two people come to hold exactly the same opinions and the same thoughts, sex stops being a meeting between two, and stops carrying either of them past themselves. Sameness is not closeness. Sameness is where the spark goes out.

She is not a clean example, and you should know that. Her lifelong open relationship with Sartre gets held up as the model. The two of them have also been accused of sexually exploiting their students — the same unequal power her books attack. What that costs the argument is yours to decide.

Your life is also not Paris. Bins, laundry, money, food: someone does each of those. Beauvoir is not banning roles, or tradition, or monogamy. She has one question about whatever arrangement you land in. Was it chosen, discussed, and chosen again — or did it arrive already written? We all play roles. What matters is how knowingly we play them.

Rilke has the shape of it: two solitudes that "protect and border and greet each other". Protect first. Border — each of you keeps an edge. Then greet.

So your job is not to hand over more of yourself. That is easy, and people will praise you for it. Ask instead what you are protecting in them — the work, the friend, the ambition you have nothing to do with — and guard it. Then ask them to guard yours, out loud, and again next year. An arrangement nobody reopens has stopped being a choice.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: You disagreed about something that mattered this month, and neither of you folded to keep the peace.
There is a plan in their life you are not part of, and it does not frighten you.
The chores are split that way because you both decided it — not because it settled in the first month and never moved.
You have reopened the arrangement at least once since you made it.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Guard the part of them that has nothing to do with you.

recall.q: Beauvoir calls total devotion the sneakiest kind of bad faith. Why is it so hard to see — and what does a couple lose by merging into one?
recall.a: It is hard to see because it never looks like self-denial; it arrives dressed as selflessness and duty. And when two people come to hold exactly the same opinions and thoughts, they lose the spark: sex stops being a meeting between two, and stops carrying either of them past themselves.

cards.title: The gene that tells a mouse it has had enough nicotine
cards.body: In mice, taking nicotine without limit was not about liking it more. One missing receptor part switched off the bad feeling that says stop. Putting the gene back into one small brain structure brought the limit back. The odd part: the lab had done most of the work before human genetics ever pointed at the gene.
cards.evidence: mouse study · alpha-5 knockout plus habenula-specific rescue · Nature 2011

sections.text:
A graduate student stands in front of their lab in 2011, holding a paper to present. Their own work runs one way: give nicotine, watch the brain, then watch what the animal does. The paper in their hand runs the other way. It starts with human DNA and walks inward.

Three years earlier, a gene called CHRNA5 had begun showing up in GWAS — scans that compare the DNA of thousands of people to find gene versions that are more common in, say, heavy smokers. CHRNA5 builds the alpha-5 subunit, one small part of a nicotinic receptor. That receptor is the docking point on brain cells where nicotine plugs in. The scans could show this gene version travelling with nicotine dependence. They could not show that it caused anything, or how.

Christie Fowler, Paul Kenny and their colleagues bred mice without the mouse version of that gene, then let the animals dose themselves. Normal mice self-adjust. As the dose on offer goes up, they take fewer hits and hold their intake roughly level. The mice without alpha-5 did not. They took far more, and raising the dose did not slow them down.

Then came the step that turned a difference into a mechanism. The team put the gene back in one place only: the medial habenula, a small structure deep in the brain. The ceiling returned. The path running from the habenula to the interpeduncular nucleus was making the unpleasant signal that says enough. Gene, circuit, behaviour — joined in one line.

The tidy version of this story is that human genetics pointed and a mouse lab followed. That student believed it for more than ten years. Then came a dinner in 2023, after Kenny gave the main lecture at a nicotine and tobacco research meeting. The two authors said most of the experiments were already finished. They had built the mice. They already understood the receptor and the habenula circuit. When the human signal arrived, they were among the few people ready to see what it meant.

GWAS now throw off signals far faster than anyone can test them. Few studies since have shown so clearly how a gene changes behaviour. This one could, because the answer was already being built before the question arrived.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: The causal work is all in mice, and there the gene was removed outright. On the human side there is only a link between a gene version and dependence, not proof of cause. And the account of how the study really began comes from one researcher's memory of a single dinner with the authors.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Risk here was not a stronger pull. It was a brake that never gripped.

recall.q: Mice without alpha-5 took far more nicotine than normal mice. What was missing — and what did putting the gene back into the medial habenula show?
recall.a: Not extra pleasure, but a stop signal. The circuit from the habenula to the interpeduncular nucleus makes an unpleasant signal that keeps normal mice holding their intake level as the dose rises. Putting the gene back into that one structure brought the limit back, linking a gene to a circuit to a behaviour.

cards.title: The AI frontier moves at the speed of money
cards.body: We read AI's pace as an engineering question. It is closer to a spending question. Each step up now costs many times more and buys little that customers notice — and Anthropic and OpenAI are preparing to sell shares to investors.

sections.text:
The last few years really did look like pure engineering, which is why the picture sticks.

Then the maths changed. Each step up in capability now costs many times more, and buys little that customers can feel. Solving a famous unsolved maths problem is a bragging right; it does not make a model steadier at dull business work. The reliability people pay for comes mostly from the software built around the model.

Then the calendar. Anthropic and OpenAI are preparing to go public — to sell shares to outside investors. Today's models already earn well even if they barely improve. "We will spend billions racing" is a harder pitch than that.

The belief survives because the pace argument always arrives dressed as safety or progress. Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, who must soon justify the spend, want the frontier paced. Nvidia's Jensen Huang, who sells the hardware for the buildout, does not. The safety worry may be sincere. It also fits the money.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The real threat to these companies may not be a rival's bigger model. It may be a much smaller one. Richard Sutton's Oak Lab is trying to build a capable model that runs on 20 watts — about what the human brain uses — and keeps learning after training, instead of freezing when training ends. Cheap AI would cut the labs' own costs. It would also let customers get the same work done without the giant data centres those labs have already paid for.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Sutton says the big-model companies may be "at risk when this eventually happens," while granting they have had "a good run." The twist: safety researchers may fear a small, self-updating model more than today's giants. It is easier to get loose from a lab, and harder to switch off.

recall.q: Each step up in model capability now costs many times more. Why does that hand the pace of the AI frontier to investors rather than engineers?
recall.a: Because the extra capability barely improves what customers actually buy — reliability comes mostly from the software built around the model. So the spending has to be justified to shareholders, especially with Anthropic and OpenAI preparing to go public. That is why the pace argument follows the money: Amodei and Altman, who must defend the spend, want the frontier paced; Huang, who sells the hardware, does not.

cards.title: Are teens worse off? The evidence may never settle it
cards.body: Youth suicide rose from around 2010, hit girls harder than boys, and hit preteen girls hardest of all — a shape the smartphone theory fits and most rival theories miss. It still has no strong evidence behind it, and one line of psychology says the causes may be too tangled for any study to sort out. Paul Bloom's answer: stop asking what the data proves, and ask what an adolescence is for.

sections.text:
The answers arrived before the question did. Paul Bloom wrote a post about teenagers and screens, and his inbox filled with people who already knew what was wrong. It's wokeness. It's cancel culture. It's capitalism crushing kids' spirits. It's climate dread, bad schools, soft parents, an economy with no room in it for them. Bloom reaches for a line Mencken never quite wrote. He knows it is a misquote and uses it anyway: for every complex problem there is an answer that is clear, simple and wrong.

So take the question cleanly. Are teenagers today worse off — and if they are, did the phones do it?

The case for yes starts with a shape in the data. Youth suicide began rising around 2010. Girls were hit harder than boys. Preteen girls were hit hardest of all. An explanation has to fit all three facts, and most don't. Wokeness has no date stamp on it. Capitalism does not single out eleven-year-old girls. The smartphone theory fits the timing, the sex and the age. Whatever else is wrong with it, that is a real point in its favour, and the rival theories cannot make it.

Now the case for no, at equal strength. The same data has parts the phone story leaves out. Suicide began falling again around 2018, especially among boys, and Bloom doubts anyone has explained why. Teenagers in many European countries are not doing as badly.

Then the deeper problem. Eric Turkheimer defends what psychologists call the gloomy prospect. The phrase comes from a 1987 paper by Robert Plomin and Denise Daniels. They asked why children in one family turn out so differently, and floated an unwelcome answer: the environment that matters may be "unsystematic, idiosyncratic, or serendipitous". Near enough to random. Plomin and Daniels called that a research dead end and went looking for tidier answers, like birth order and friends. Turkheimer thinks the dead end is simply the truth.

His point is not that behaviour is magic. It is that behaviour comes out of a huge web of causes that interact and loop back on each other, and the web is different for every person. A mess too big to untangle. Bloom extends it to whole countries: a national trend is made of the same mess. And the smartphone case has produced no strong evidence anyway.

So what would decide it? Bloom's own list is the test: one account that explains the 2010 rise, the girls, the preteens, the 2018 fall among boys, and Europe. Nothing manages all of that yet. The gloomy prospect says something harder to hear — nothing may ever manage it.

Bloom does not split the difference. He rejects the better-safe-than-sorry case for bans. The burden sits on whoever proposes the ban. Phones plainly give kids pleasure, or no ban would be needed. And a fourteen-year-old is not a four-year-old. Yet he stays on the fence, because his sympathy for critics like Jonathan Haidt and Jean Twenge never rested on suicide graphs. It rests on what he thinks adolescence is for — books, sport, art, being outside, films, dating, goofing around with friends, the odd hour with your parents. Picture a daughter whose only companions are AI, or a son whose every free hour goes to porn. Would you wait for a meta-analysis, a study that pools all the other studies? Bloom thinks that question — what makes a life well lived — matters more than the psychology studies everyone, himself included, is obsessed with.

sections.label: The strongest objection
sections.text: Bloom's best card against bans: kids like their phones. If they didn't, you would not need a ban. The strongest reply, which he raises himself — maybe teenagers don't much like Instagram, and stay because all their friends are there. That makes it a collective action problem: a trap no single kid can walk out of alone. Then the case for a rule covering everyone gets much stronger. Bloom thinks the point is overstated. Polls on how teens feel about social media are mixed, and it doesn't apply to watching TikTok videos anyway.

sections.label: Key takeaways
sections.text:
The data has a shape: a rise around 2010, girls harder hit, preteen girls hardest. The smartphone theory fits that shape; the popular alternatives don't.

The same data has gaps — the fall after 2018, mainly among boys, and the milder picture across much of Europe. Nobody has explained either.

The gloomy prospect: behaviour comes from a web of causes that loop back on each other and differ for every person. No future study may untangle it.

Bloom's own argument for limiting phones runs on none of the harm data. It runs on which activities he thinks make an adolescence worth having.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The question was never only whether phones harm children. It was what we think a childhood is for.

recall.q: Bloom's case for limiting teen phone use does not rest on the suicide data. What does it rest on instead?
recall.a: On what he thinks an adolescence is for — books, sport, art, being outside, films, dating, time with friends and the odd hour with parents. The question becomes whether hours of TikTok crowd out the things worth doing, and no study or meta-analysis can settle that for you.

cards.title: Sleeptalking: why it happens and what it can't reveal
cards.body: The brain does not switch off all at once. The parts that make speech can still be running after the parts that keep your mouth still have gone under — so words get out. In sleep labs, what a person says during REM matches their dream about 80% of the time. But nobody has ever shown you can talk a sleeper into giving up a secret.
cards.evidence: multiple studies cited · sleep-lab observation · sample sizes not given

sections.text:
The most common word people say in their sleep is no. About 5% of all words spoken while asleep are that one word.

Most sleeptalking is not words at all — mumbles, laughs, whispers. When real language does come out, it is often a question, sometimes swearing. Sleeptalkers are rarely polite. They sound like someone in the middle of an argument.

Why does the mouth move at all?

The brain does not fall asleep all at once. Scientists think the speech parts stay switched on while the parts that normally keep your mouth still have already gone under. The words get out because the guard is asleep.

Are they saying their dream out loud?

Often, yes. REM sleep — rapid eye movement, about a quarter of the night, where the vivid dreams live — is the stage researchers can check. In sleep labs, what a sleeptalker says during REM matches their dream at that moment about 80% of the time. That is why the pauses sound so real. You may be hearing one half of a conversation inside the dream.

Can you get a secret out of them?

You can get them to answer. Researchers find that about half the time, a sleeptalker replies to a question or a remark said out loud. But no study has ever shown anyone using this to pull out something a person was hiding.

Does it mean something is wrong?

Almost never. More than two-thirds of people sleeptalk at some point. It belongs to a family called parasomnias — things your body does or your mind goes through while asleep, like sleepwalking and night terrors. These count as disorders only when they happen often enough to cause real trouble. Sleeptalking does raise your odds of the other parasomnias, and it shows up more when you are overtired.

So why do children do it far more than adults?

Here the answers run out. Children have more slow-wave sleep — the deep, heavy stage outside REM — and that share shrinks as you grow older, so the shift may explain it. But researchers do not really know why, and there is little sleeptalking research to work from. The brain falling asleep in pieces is the best explanation anyone has for why you talk. Nobody has one for why you stop.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: These numbers come from separate studies. The 80% dream-match figure comes from sleep labs, where people are watched overnight — a small and unusual setting. One study also found that sleeptalkers get more than an hour and a half less sleep a night than non-sleeptalkers, and about half as much REM. That is a difference between two groups, not proof that one causes the other.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Sleep is not a switch being flipped. It is lights going out one at a time — and sometimes the mouth is the last one still on.

recall.q: A sleeptalker's words match their dream about 80% of the time, and they answer questions about half the time. So why can't you use that to get a secret out of them?
recall.a: Both findings are real, but no study has ever shown a sleeper being steered into revealing something they were hiding. Sleeptalking leaks the dream, not the guarded thought — and most of the time it is not even words.

cards.title: If humanity had 200 years left, could life still matter?
cards.body: Tim Mulgan changes one detail in a famous thought experiment: humanity's end is certain, but two hundred years away. That gap gives us time to rebuild what we live for. His answer is that meaning survives only if we build shared projects that still feel worth doing to the very last generation.

sections.text:
Something explodes many light years away. Nobody on Earth feels it. Then the astronomers finish the numbers and announce that in about two hundred years, every living thing here will be gone.

That is the setup of Tim Mulgan's Philosophy for an Ending World, and everything turns on those two hundred years. Samuel Scheffler got there first, in 2013: imagine everyone stops being able to have children, and humanity ends soon. He guessed we would stop believing anything mattered. Most of what we care about quietly assumes people will keep existing. Take that away and we sink into anomie, a flat state where nothing feels worth doing.

Mulgan pushes the deadline back. Certain, but not soon. Two hundred years is enough time to adapt, and that opens a real argument. His Perennial Pessimist says life never had meaning anyway, and would rather no one else was born. His Presentist says plenty of good things survive, because they never needed the future. His Post-Cataclysmic Pessimist says the deadline ruins everything, at least given how we think about meaning now. Mulgan backs a fourth view: multigenerationalism.

It gives the pessimists their hard point. Meaning does need future people. Even small, here-and-now activities take their point from traditions handed forward. But those traditions, Mulgan argues, can be cut loose from the idea that humanity runs on forever. Build shared projects with an end date.

The trap is the last generation. If the final humans cannot live meaningfully, it was wrong to make them. Then the generation before them was wrong to have children, and so on back down the line, an "intergenerational Ponzi scheme". Three careful chapters argue the way out. Having children stays right if the projects are genuine, if the next lives can be at least as good as ours, and if the last people can find meaning in finishing humanity's story well.

The strongest move follows. Our values assume an endless future, so handing them down unchanged would cheat our descendants. New values have to be invented, slowly, across generations. Mulgan's proof that this can be done is Plenty Coups, the Crow chief in Jonathan Lear's Radical Hope, who rebuilt what courage could mean for his people after the wars that had defined it ended.

The book overreaches by carrying too much: religion, uploading the last minds into virtual worlds, what a final utopia might look like, all in dense academic detail that will lose most readers. The range shows how rich the idea is, but a shorter version would reach a far bigger audience. Read it if you have patience for argument, and read it for the closing point. You do not have to believe extinction is near. You only have to believe your descendants' world will be unlike anything humanity has lived through.

sections.label: The weak link
sections.text: The weak link is the idea the book leans on hardest. Take philosophy. Part of what makes it meaningful is joining a conversation that will outlast you. But would it really matter less if you knew that conversation ended in two hundred years? Is it not enough that some people alive now care about it the way you do? Mulgan needs the answer to be no, and he never argues that at length. The phrase "a fitting end" for humanity's story is soft in the same way. It feels obviously important, and it is never pinned down.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: Scheffler's original case: if extinction comes soon, our confidence that anything matters collapses.
Mulgan's one change: the end is certain but two centuries off, which leaves time to adapt.
Multigenerationalism: meaning needs future people, but not infinitely many of them.
The catch: the last generation must find their own lives meaningful, or bringing them into existence was wrong.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A life that matters may not need humanity to go on forever. It may only need the next pair of hands, and a story someone is willing to finish.

recall.q: Mulgan agrees with the pessimists that meaning depends on future people. So how does he get meaningful lives back once the end is certain?
recall.a: By cutting shared, handed-down meaning loose from the idea that humanity lasts forever. Projects can still run across generations and have an end date, as long as the last generation can find meaning in bringing them, and humanity's story, to a fitting close.

cards.title: Where you live shows up on your brain scan
cards.body: Researchers took 2,826 ordinary hospital brain scans, all with no visible disease. Then they added one thing the scan could not know: how poor the patient's postal area was. Brains from the poorest areas looked about three years older than their owners. They held less tissue, and carried more of the bright marks left by failing blood vessels.
cards.evidence: single study · n=2,826 · retrospective cross-sectional clinical MRI · ZIP-code-level deprivation index · adjusted for ag

sections.text:
A brain MRI does not record an address. It records shape. How much grey and white matter is there, and where the small bright spots sit — the places blood stopped reaching.

Researchers at the University of Wisconsin pulled 2,826 such scans. All came from ordinary patients who passed through hospital and community clinics between January and June 2024. All were clean: no visible brain disease. Ages ran from 18 to 96, average 53. Then the team attached something the scan itself could not know — where the patient lived.

The tool for that is the Area Deprivation Index, or ADI. It scores a small census area on 17 markers of income, housing quality, jobs and schooling, drawn from a 2023 national survey. It knows nothing about you as a person. It knows your postal area.

Two measurements carried the result. The first is the brain age gap. Software guesses how old a brain looks, then you subtract the person's real age. Zero means the brain looks its age. A positive number means it looks older. Patients in the poorest neighbourhoods carried a gap about 2.7 years wider than everyone else. Ranked within the state instead of the country, it was 3 years.
