Their total brain volume was smaller too, after every measure was scaled to skull size and adjusted for age and sex.

The second is white matter hyperintensities: bright patches where small blood vessels have failed and the tissue behind them has been starved. The senior author, John-Paul Yu, calls them "the footprints of cardiovascular damage in the brain" — damage left by things like high blood pressure, poor sleep and constant stress. Poorer neighbourhoods had more of them. Both markers matter outside the scanner. Older-looking brains have been tied to heart and blood vessel disease, loss of thinking ability, and mental illness. The bright patches have been tied to memory loss, trouble with planning, and dementia.

The quieter finding is the one to hold on to. The team also checked whether those bright patches came with shrinkage elsewhere. In the poorest neighbourhoods, that link was steeper. The same load of vessel damage sat with a smaller striatum — structures deep in the middle of the brain — and a smaller dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the outer front region behind and beside the forehead. Not just more damage. Damage that travelled with more loss.

Each person was scanned once, and each already had some reason to be in a scanner. So nothing here shows that a neighbourhood ages a brain. What the authors want is narrower and more usable. Numbers like these could work as a hard marker of where disadvantage has settled into tissue — readable years before anyone forgets a name, and available to a health system deciding where to send help first.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text:
2,826 patients — 1,732 women, 1,094 men — each scanned once. Deprivation was scored from the postal area, then ranked two ways: against the whole country, and within the state. Only 116 patients landed in the poorest national band, and 129 in the poorest state band.

Against everyone else, that group showed a brain age gap wider by 2.72 years (national) and 3.02 years (state), total brain volume lower by 6.33 and 7.46 millilitres after scaling for skull size, and more white matter damage. All at p below .01, meaning the pattern is unlikely to be chance. Inside that group, the link between vessel damage and smaller striatal and prefrontal volumes was stronger than elsewhere.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
These are links found in a single snapshot, not proof that a neighbourhood ages a brain. The index is geographic. Nobody's own income, schooling, blood pressure or habits was measured, so personal circumstances may be carrying part of what looks like a neighbourhood effect. The models adjusted only for age and sex.

And the headline rests on a thin slice: 116 of 2,826 patients, about 4 percent, all of them people already inside a hospital scanner for some reason of their own.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The scan had no field for an address. It turned out not to need one.

recall.q: The deprivation score came only from the patient's postal area, never from the patient. What can the three-year brain age gap tell you, and what can it not?
recall.a: It can tell you that people from the poorest areas had brains that looked about three years older, once age and sex were accounted for. It cannot tell you the neighbourhood caused it. No one's own income, schooling or health was measured, and each brain was scanned only once, so a person's own circumstances could be carrying part of the pattern.

cards.title: Nerves are steered from the cell body, not the growing tip
cards.body: For decades scientists thought a growing nerve fibre finds its own way, reading chemical signs at its own tip. A new study says the cell body is steering. At each checkpoint on the route it switches whole groups of genes on and off, changing which sensors the tip even has. That turns the hardest part of nerve repair — aiming a regrown fibre — into a genetics problem.
cards.evidence: single study · rodent neurons · 12,000+ cells profiled · single-cell RNA sequencing · 4 developmental stages

sections.text:
Wiggle your toe. The cell that gave the order sits at the base of your spine. Its single long wire runs down your whole leg to reach the muscle. That wire is called an axon. Before you were born, it had to grow that whole distance and find the right muscle at the end, through a body that was still changing shape around it.

Billions of axons do this. For decades the standard view was that the growing tip does all the deciding. The tip is far from the cell body, and the chemical landscape it crawls through shifts fast. So it must read the local signs and choose for itself. The cell body was the factory. The tip was the driver.

A study from the Carney Institute for Brain Science at Brown University, published in PNAS, says the cell body has been driving too.

Long axons do not travel in one go. They stop at checkpoints and turn toward the next goal. The team studied the neurons that make one of the sharpest turns in the body: spinal commissural neurons, which link the left and right halves of the nervous system. Their axons cross the middle line of the spinal cord, then swing hard away from it.

When the axon reaches that midline, something happens back in the nucleus, the part of the cell body that holds the genes. Whole groups of genes switch on. Others switch off. That changes which guidance receptors the cell builds and ships out to the tip. Receptors are the proteins the tip uses to feel the chemical signs around it. The tip does not get smarter. It gets a different set of senses. With new receptors, the same midline that pulled it in now reads as something to leave.

Alexander Jaworski, who led the work, said neurons turn whole blocks of genes on and off so their axons can grow through different stretches of the route. His word for the result: "surprising." The old picture made guidance a local conversation between one molecule and one tip. Now it is a program, run from the cell body, with the tip as the place the program gets used.

That matters most where nerves are broken. After a stroke or a spinal cord injury, growth is no longer the wall. Engineers can already get a cut axon to sprout and extend. Getting it back to the right partner cell is the part nobody has solved. If the aiming instructions sit in the nucleus as a set of genes that can be turned on, that is a target you can at least imagine reaching.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: These neurons had been a favourite model for axon guidance for years. But nobody could reach them genetically, so nobody could watch the whole process. The team built a custom genetic tool to pull commissural neurons out of rodents at four points in development. Then they ran single-cell RNA sequencing — reading which genes are active inside one cell at a time — on more than 12,000 neurons, and worked out when each neuron was born. The result is an atlas: a map of which genes are running in which neuron, and when.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: One study, in rodent embryos, watching normal development — not injured adults, and not humans. It shows the gene program shifts as the axon crosses the midline, and that the shift drives the crossing. It does not show that switching those genes on in a damaged spinal cord will send a regrown axon home. The neurons were also far from uniform: the shared switch sits on top of a lot of cell-to-cell variation, which the atlas maps but does not explain. No therapy follows from this yet.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The wire was never finding its own way. It was being told, one stretch at a time.

recall.q: The tip still does the crawling. So what changed when the axon reached the midline, and why does that matter for nerve repair?
recall.a: In the cell body's nucleus, whole groups of genes switched on and off. That changed which guidance receptors were shipped out to the tip. The tip did not get smarter; it got a new set of senses, so the midline that had pulled it in now read as something to leave. If aiming is a gene program, it is something you might switch on — and aiming, not growth, is the unsolved half of nerve repair.

cards.title: Two brain patches fight over risk before your hand moves
cards.body: Doctors recorded from electrodes already sitting inside six people's brains while they played a game about bombs and treasure. Two patches of the orbitofrontal cortex, about two centimetres apart, swung back and forth between go and stop. Whichever one was ahead half a second before the hand moved predicted the choice. The old picture — a decision as a dial turning slowly toward a line — may be wrong.
cards.evidence: single study · n=6 · intracranial electrode recordings during a video-game task

sections.text:
Patients sat in hospital beds with wires running out of their heads, playing Candy Crush.

Clara Starkweather, a chief resident in neurosurgery at UCSF, noticed them. The usual tool for her question is fMRI, a scanner that tracks blood flow, and it was failing her twice over. The brain region she cared about sits close to the air-filled sinuses behind the eyes, which bend the scanner's magnetic field, so the picture comes out blurred. And volunteers doing a flat little task in a scanner were "falling asleep". The patients with the phones were not bored. So she built a game.

What the recordings show is solid. The target region is the orbitofrontal cortex, long suspected of being where the brain weighs a reward against its risk. Before a player went for the treasure, two neighbouring parts of it moved in opposite directions: activity rose in the inner part and fell in the outer part. When one spiked, the other dropped. Watch which side is ahead and you can call the choice 500 milliseconds — half a second — before the hand moves.

What that winning signal actually is stays open. A decision, or a leaning? The two patches did not settle smoothly. Before a choice they flipped back and forth between a go state and a stop state. On easy trials — treasure, no bombs — go won almost at once. On hard ones the flicker ran on until one side held. So catching the leader half a second early may mean watching the choice get made. Or it may mean watching the last of several near-choices, one of which happened to stick. A recording cannot tell those apart. It is also why the half-second head start says less about you than it sounds.

The live disagreement is about shape. Standard models of choice say the brain piles up evidence until it crosses a line, like a dial turning smoothly. Starkweather and Robert Knight of UC Berkeley modelled their recordings and say it looks nothing like that — more like "a switch flipping back and forth" between two extremes until one holds. Edward Chang, the UCSF surgeon who shares senior authorship, makes the narrower claim: nobody could measure this region live in a human brain until now.

Settling it would take pushing, not watching. The same paper argues that electrical stimulation of this region, already used for severe mental illness, has given mixed results because doctors treated it as one lump — when the stop zone and the go zone are two centimetres apart. Too much avoid looks like depression, anxiety and OCD. Too much approach looks like gambling and addiction. So aim current at one patch mid-flicker. If the choice changes, the flicker is the decision. If the hand goes where it was always going, the signal was only a report.

sections.label: The setup
sections.text: Six people already had electrodes inside their skulls, placed temporarily to find the source of their epilepsy before surgery. They volunteered to play. The game drops you into a maze of hallways; some corridors are lined with explosives, and glowing chests of rubies sit at the end. Each round narrows to one crossroad: walk the bomb-lined hallway for the rubies, or turn away and keep the score you have. Activity was recorded throughout on a millisecond timescale. Published in Nature Neuroscience.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Six people, all with epilepsy severe enough to need electrodes in the brain. Those electrodes were placed for their surgery, not for this experiment. The danger on offer was points, not injury. This is one study — a first measurement, not a finished map.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Half a second of warning is not half a second of certainty. The brain spends most of it changing its mind.

recall.q: Watching the two patches tells you the choice half a second before the hand moves. Why does that not show the decision was already made?
recall.a: Because the patches were still flipping. On hard choices they swung between go and stop until one side held, so the leader you catch may be the last of several near-choices rather than a settled decision. A recording shows which signal wins, not whether it causes the move or only reports it.

cards.title: India's new UPI fee is now before the Supreme Court
cards.body: The government has put a charge on UPI merchant payments above ₹2,000. A public interest case now before the Supreme Court says shops will not carry that charge in the end. They will raise prices, so the customer does.

sections.text:
What is MDR? Merchant discount rate — the cut a business pays out of each digital payment it takes. The money goes to the banks and payment firms that move it.

Why did UPI feel free? Merchants paid no such cut on UPI. The government has now brought in charges on merchant payments above ₹2,000.

What does the case ask? A public interest litigation — a case filed for the general public, not over one person's loss — is challenging those charges. The Supreme Court will review them.

Who actually pays? On paper, the shop. The petition says that will not hold. A shop can add the fee to its prices, and then customers carry it. That claim, not the size of the fee, is the case.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Strike down the charge and the cost does not vanish. Someone still has to pay to move the money. Nobody in this case has said who.

recall.q: The new charge is billed to merchants, not to the person paying. So why does the petition call it a burden on ordinary citizens?
recall.a: Because a shop can pass the cost on. If businesses raise prices to cover the fee, customers end up paying it even though it never shows on their bill. That claim is what the Supreme Court has to judge.

cards.title: China went quiet on Taiwan while Xi purged his generals
cards.body: Xi Jinping has removed almost the whole top of China's military. Two analysts say the new calm between Washington and Beijing is cover for the repairs.

sections.text:
Two former defense ministers got suspended death sentences in May. The party expelled He Weidong, a vice chairman of the Central Military Commission. On Aug. 28, 2026 the national legislature removed Zhang Youxia, the commission's senior vice chairman. Of the seven officers Xi picked for that body in 2022, one still serves beside him.

Pressure on Taiwan fell over the same months. China had run a big exercise around the island in the first half of every year since 2023. In 2026 it ran none. Writing in War on the Rocks, Christopher Nye — a pseudonym — and Charles Sun say this is why Beijing wanted a truce with Washington. A force that has just lost its commanders cannot risk complex joint drills that would show the mess. The quiet lets Beijing sell a forced lull as a peace offer.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 27 full general and admiral posts across the army and armed police — only 6 have a confirmed holder
About 20 are run by lieutenant generals as stand-ins
Taiwan detected less than half as many Chinese fighter jets as a year earlier
Military budget up about 7% this year, the slowest rise since 2021

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The truce is worth more to Beijing than to Washington, so Beijing now takes pressure it would normally refuse. But it calls this stability the guide for the next three years and beyond — into the next US president's first year. Permits already granted and arms packages already put off are hard to undo. The authors expect the rebuilt force to arrive on time.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Xi is due at the White House on Sept. 24. China's pause on rare-earth export controls ends Nov. 10, 2026. The authors expect Beijing to offer rare earths as the price of another stretch of quiet.

recall.q: Chinese military activity around Taiwan dropped sharply in 2026. Why do the authors read that as weakness, not restraint?
recall.a: Xi has emptied the top of the command chain — only six of 27 full-general posts have a confirmed holder. A force in that state cannot risk big joint drills that would show the mess. So the lull is partly forced, and the truce lets Beijing present it as peace.
